Henry V. A history play by William Shakespeare written around fifteen ninety-eight or fifteen ninety-nine that depicts the ascension and military triumph of King Henry the Fifth of England, culminating in his legendary victory at the Battle of Agincourt in fourteen fifteen. The play traces Henry's transformation from the dissolute Prince Hal into a disciplined warrior-king who unites his fractious nobles and army through sheer force of will and rhetoric. It is Shakespeare's most patriotic work, a meditation on the costs and glories of kingship, the nature of military leadership, and the paradoxes of justified warfare.

Henry the Fifth inherits the throne after his father Henry the Fourth's death. His reformation from wild youth to serious monarch is Shakespeare's theme of maturation and duty. The Battle of Agincourt in fourteen fifteen is the play's climax. Henry's outnumbered English archers devastate the French nobility in a stunning victory that solidifies his claim to French territory and his legend as a warrior-king.

Henry's famous rallying speeches are among Shakespeare's greatest rhetorical achievements, especially the St. Crispin's Day oration before Agincourt. These speeches galvanize his troops through appeals to honor, brotherhood, and English identity. The play's comic subplot involves soldiers and common men like Bardolph, Fluellen, and Pistol. Their cowardice, larceny, and stumbling heroism provide counterpoint to the kings' grand designs, humanizing the war's costs.

Katharine of France, the French princess, becomes Henry's romantic interest. Their marriage is negotiated as part of the peace settlement, merging personal affection with political alliance. The play wrestles with the ethics of warfare. Henry must weigh his soldiers' lives against his territorial ambitions. The text does not entirely endorse his ruthlessness, including his execution of prisoners and the destruction of towns.

Henry embodies an ideal of just, effective kingship grounded in both martial prowess and rhetorical power. Henry V completes the second tetralogy of Shakespeare's history plays. The historical Battle of Agincourt defines the play's action and Henry's legend. The central theme is kingship itself. History plays balance personal drama with historical events. England is the play's stage and it is deeply invested in English national identity and patriotic mythology. War is examined both as glorious and destructive. The play offers no simple moral about military conflict but instead presents the complexity and ambiguity of military leadership and national ambition.
